A school day lasts 6 hours. A working week has 5 school days. Explain step by step how to find the total number of minutes a child spends in school in one week.

A friend says, "To convert 2 days and 3 hours into hours, I will do 2 + 3 = 5 hours, because I just add the two numbers." Evaluate whether this method is correct, explain what is wrong, and give the correct solution.
A train journey from Chennai to Kolkata takes 1 day and 5 hours. Calculate the total duration of the journey in hours. Then convert just the 5 hours part into minutes and state it.

Design a simple time-conversion puzzle for your classmate using a real-life Indian situation. Include a mixed-unit time, ask for the answer in a single smaller unit, and write out the full solution with working.
What is data collection? Name two ways by which you can collect simple real-life data, and list the two things that every pictograph must always have.

Riya surveyed 12 classmates about their favourite sport. Her table shows: Cricket -- 5, Football -- 4, Tennis -- 3. She then drew a pictograph but forgot to write the key. Explain why her pictograph is incomplete and what problem this could cause for someone reading it.

A student says, "Once I have made a neat two-column table of my survey data, there is no need to make a pictograph because the table already shows all the information." Evaluate this statement. Do you agree? Give a balanced argument.
The table below shows the number of children absent in Class 3 each day for a week. Draw a pictograph for this data. Make sure to include a title and a key.

Design a short survey that you could conduct in your classroom. Decide on the question, the categories, and how you will record the answers. Then describe how you would organise the results in a table and represent them as a pictograph.
What does it mean to classify data, and what does it mean to compare data? Name the three comparison words we use after counting the categories.

A class survey of favourite sports gave this table: Cricket -- 6, Football -- 4, Kabaddi -- 2. Explain step by step how you would classify and compare this data, and state which sport is liked by the most and which by the fewest children.

A student looks at a pictograph showing lunch boxes in class -- Rice (8 pictures), Roti (6 pictures), Sandwich (3 pictures) -- and says, "Sandwich is the most common lunch because the sandwich pictures are drawn biggest." Evaluate this answer. Is the student correct? Explain what the student did wro

Here is a table of crayons sorted by colour: Red -- 9, Blue -- 5, Green -- 5, Yellow -- 7. Answer three questions: (a) Which colour has the most crayons? (b) Which two colours have an equal number of crayons? (c) Which colour has the fewest crayons? Give a reason from the data for each answer.

Design your own classify-and-compare activity for your classroom using any collection you can find (for example, leaves, buttons, erasers, or lunch boxes). Describe the collection, the feature you will use to classify it, the categories you will make, and three comparison questions you would ask a f
What is the correct way to write a tally count of nine using the grouping-in-fives convention, and why is the diagonal fifth mark used?

Twenty classmates were asked their favourite fruit. The tally marks are: mango -- "|||| ||||" (ten), apple -- "||||" (five), banana -- "||||" (five). Explain how you would convert these tallies into a pictograph and state what the pictograph would show.

A student looked at a tally table showing pets owned by children in a class -- dog: "|||| ||" (seven), cat: "||||" (five), fish: "||" (two) -- and wrote the conclusion: "Dogs are the best pet." Evaluate whether this is a good conclusion and explain what a correct conclusion should look like.

Record the following data using tally marks grouped in fives, then draw a pictograph and write two conclusions. Data: In a week, the number of sunny days was 4, cloudy days was 2, and rainy days was 1.

Design a small survey that you could carry out in your classroom to find out which game your classmates like best. Describe how you would record the data using tally marks, how you would turn it into a pictograph, and what conclusions you might be able to draw.
Look at the pattern trianglecircletrianglecircletrianglecircle... What is the unit of repeat? Extend the pattern by two more units.

Two students look at the pattern trianglecirclesquaretrianglecirclesquaretrianglecirclesquare... Ananya says the unit of repeat is 'trianglecirclesquaretrianglecirclesquare'. Rohan says the unit is 'trianglecirclesquare'. Who is correct and why?
A friend says, "The pattern 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12... has a unit of repeat, and the unit is '2, 4, 6'." Evaluate whether this statement is correct.

Create your own pattern using vegetable cut-outs of ladyfinger and potato stamped with ink. State the unit of repeat and write out the first six items of your pattern. Then extend it by two more units.
Design an original pattern using three different shapes of your choice. Write down the unit of repeat, build the pattern for three full units, and explain how a friend would extend it.
State the rule for comparing two four-digit numbers using place value, and explain what ascending and descending order mean.
Compare 3456 and 3462 and explain exactly which place value decides which number is greater. Why do we not stop at the hundreds place?

A student says, "3888 is greater than 4111 because 3888 has bigger digits in the hundreds, tens, and ones places." Evaluate whether this claim is correct and explain the correct way to compare these two numbers.
Arrange the following numbers in both ascending and descending order, showing which place value you used: 5234, 5239, 5200, 5290.

Design a small game using number cards (1 to 9, 10 to 90, 100 to 900, and 1000 to 9000) that helps a Class 3 child practise comparing four-digit numbers and arranging them in ascending and descending order. Describe how the game is played and what the child learns.
What is a rule in a number pattern? Give one example of a growing rule and one example of a shrinking rule, and write the next three terms for each.
Look at the pattern 5, 8, 11, 14, ... Explain step by step how you would identify the rule, and then extend the pattern by the next three terms.

A child looks at the pattern 30, 25, 20, 15, ... and says, "The rule is add 5, because the jump between the numbers is 5. The next three terms are 20, 25, 30." Evaluate whether this answer is correct, and explain what the child has done wrong and how to fix it.
A shape pattern begins with a triangle (3 sides), then a square (4 sides), then a pentagon (5 sides), then a hexagon (6 sides). Identify the rule and predict the next two shapes in the pattern.

Make your own growing number pattern that uses the rule "add 4". Write the first five terms of your pattern, then write the next three terms. Finally, explain the rule in your own words as if you were teaching it to a younger friend.
Using the digits 3, 7, 1, 9 without repetition, form the greatest and smallest 4-digit numbers. Explain the rule you followed.

Using the digits 4, 0, 2 with repetition allowed to form a 4-digit number, the greatest is 4444 and the smallest is 2000. Explain why the smallest is NOT 0000 and why 0 cannot be placed in the thousands place.

A student says, "To form the greatest 4-digit number from the digits 8, 6, 5, 2 without repetition, I can write 8265 because it starts with the biggest digit 8, so it must be the greatest." Evaluate whether this claim is correct.
Using the digits 5, 8, 2, 6 without repetition, form the greatest and smallest 4-digit numbers. Then write the expanded form of the greatest number.

Design a number-card game for a group of four Class 3 children that helps them discover how to form the greatest and smallest 4-digit numbers from given digits. Describe the cards, the rules, and what the children will learn.
Explain what carrying over and borrowing mean in three-digit addition and subtraction, and why we always start from the ones column.
Work out 523 - 187 step by step, explaining each borrow. Then verify your answer by addition.

A student solves 803 - 358 and writes the answer as 555. She says, "I borrowed 1 from the hundreds for the ones column, so the 8 became 7, and then I subtracted normally: 7 - 3 = 4 in hundreds, 0 - 5 I just wrote 5, and 13 - 8 = 5 in ones, giving 455 -- but my friend got 445." Evaluate her working,
A shop has 468 marbles in one jar and 279 in another. The shopkeeper sells 325 marbles in a day. How many marbles are left in total? Show all working with carries and borrows, and verify.

Design a short word problem set in an Indian market that requires both addition with regrouping in the tens and subtraction with borrowing across a zero. Provide the full worked solution with verification.
Using the standard algorithm, add 356 + 247 by place value columns. Show each step and state the final sum.
In subtracting 600 - 248, explain why we cannot borrow directly from the tens column and describe exactly what we do instead.

A student solves 538 + 276 and writes the answer as 704. He says, "I added 8 + 6 = 14, wrote 4 and carried 1; then 3 + 7 = 10, wrote 0 and carried 1; then 5 + 2 = 7, so 704." Evaluate whether his method and answer are correct.
Subtract 245 from 700 using the standard algorithm. Show all borrowing steps and give the final difference.

Design a short word problem set in an Indian market that requires adding two three-digit numbers with carrying in both the ones and tens columns, and then subtracting a three-digit number involving borrowing across a zero. State the numbers, solve both using the standard algorithm, and explain each
What two steps must you follow to solve a single-step story or visual problem involving three-digit numbers, and which clue words tell you to add versus subtract?
A fair has 256 red balloons and 189 blue balloons. The question asks "How many balloons in all?" Explain why addition is the correct operation, then compute the answer showing regrouping.

A student reads the problem "Rohan had 500 rupees. He bought a bag for 325 rupees. How much money is left with him?" and writes 500 + 325 = 825. Evaluate whether this approach is correct, explain what the student did wrong, and show the correct solution with full working.

A picture shows one basket with 175 mangoes and another basket with 218 mangoes. The label asks "How many mangoes altogether?" Set up the calculation, compute the answer with regrouping where needed, and state the answer with its unit.
Write your own single-step story problem about a visit to a shop that requires subtraction of two three-digit numbers with regrouping, then solve it showing all working.
Construct the multiplication table of 7 up to 7 x 10 using repeated addition, showing each addition step.
Explain the pattern hidden in the table of 9 and use it to find 9 x 7 without reciting the whole table.

A classmate says, "The table of 4 is the hardest because there is no pattern -- I just have to memorise all ten facts." Evaluate this statement. Is the classmate correct? Give a balanced view and then state your judgement.

Riya has 6 boxes, and each box holds 7 pencils. Use the multiplication table of 7 to find how many pencils she has in total. Show which fact from the table you used and check your answer using repeated addition.

Design your own "pattern card" for the table of 10 that a younger child could use to learn the table. Describe what would be on the card and explain why each feature would help the child remember the facts.
Write the place value chart for a 6-digit number in the Indian system and state the value of each place.
Explain why 1,00,000 is the smallest 6-digit number and why 9,99,999 is the largest. Why can a number like 99,999 not be a 6-digit number?

A student says, "The number 2,45,318 and the number 245,318 are the same number, just written with the comma in a different place." Evaluate this statement. Is the student correct? Give a balanced view of what is right and what is wrong in the statement.

The price of a small car is "four lakh fifty-five thousand seven hundred rupees". Write this amount in numerals using the Indian system, place each digit in the correct place in the place value chart, and give one more real-life example of a 6-digit number.

Design a simple classroom activity using number cards (digits 0 to 9) that helps children build, read and write 6-digit numbers in the Indian system. Describe the steps and give one sample number the children might build.
Add 2345 and 1678 by regrouping, showing each step. Then verify your answer.
Subtract 5000 - 2347 and explain why you must borrow all the way from the thousands column instead of borrowing from the tens or hundreds column.

A student says, "When I add 2345 and 1678, I can start from the thousands column because addition is the same in any order, so 2 + 1 = 3, 3 + 6 = 9, 4 + 7 = 11, 5 + 8 = 13, and the answer is 39113." Evaluate whether this method is correct and explain what the student has misunderstood.

A school in Jaipur collected Rs 4650 during a charity drive and spent Rs 2890 on buying blankets for the poor. How much money is left with the school? Show the column working, estimate the answer first, and verify your answer by addition.

Design a story problem set in an Indian market that requires both addition and subtraction of four-digit numbers, with at least one step needing regrouping. Solve it step by step and verify each step.
Construct and write the complete multiplication table of 6 from 6 x 1 up to 6 x 10, and state the strategy you used.
Explain why the table of 8 is double the table of 4, and use this relationship to find 8 x 6 without counting in eights.

A classmate says, "I will just memorise all the tables from 2 to 10 by chanting them every morning. I do not need to build them with sticks or look for patterns." Evaluate this approach and explain whether it is a good strategy for the long term.
Using the digit pattern of the table of 9, write the products from 9 x 1 to 9 x 10 and verify that the digits of each product add up to 9.
Design your own way to construct the table of 7 using a real-life example with equal groups, and show how you would write it as a multiplication table.
Multiply 34 x 6 using the standard algorithm and explain each step, including the carry.
Explain why, when multiplying 23 x 12 using the standard algorithm, the partial product 23 x 1 is written as 230 and shifted one place to the left, not as 23.
A student says, "The lattice method and the standard algorithm give different answers, so one of them must be wrong." Evaluate this statement.
Multiply 123 x 4 using the standard algorithm, and then multiply 45 x 23 using the lattice method. Show all working.

Design a short word problem set in an Indian market that requires multiplying a three-digit number by a one-digit number, and solve it using both the standard algorithm and the lattice method to show they match.
Name the four terms dividend, divisor, quotient, and remainder, and state the rule that connects them. Use the example 45 / 6 = 7 remainder 3.
Divide 20 by 3 using repeated subtraction. Show every step and explain why you stop where you do. Then verify your answer.

A student says, "To divide 45 by 6, I can use the multiplication fact 6 x 8 = 48, so 45 / 6 = 8 remainder 3, because 45 - 48 = -3 and I take the difference as 3." Evaluate whether this method and answer are correct, and explain the right approach.
Divide 24 by 4 using the pictorial method. Describe exactly what you would draw and how you would count the answer. Then check the result using a multiplication fact.

Design a real-life story problem set in an Indian classroom that requires dividing 45 biscuits among packets of 6 each. State the dividend, divisor, quotient, and remainder, and explain what the remainder means in the story.
Name the four operations used to solve real life situations and state one everyday clue that tells you to use each operation.
A shopkeeper has 6 boxes of candles, each box containing 15 candles. He sells 70 candles. How many candles are left? Explain which operation you use at each step and why.

A student reads the problem "A water tank holds 250 litres. 135 litres are used. How many more litres need to be added to fill it completely?" and writes 250 + 135 = 385 litres. Evaluate whether this answer is correct, explain the error, and give the correct solution.
Solve this problem involving money with two operations: "A school bought 4 boxes of chalk, each costing Rs45. The shopkeeper gave a discount of Rs20 on the total. How much did the school pay?"
Write your own real life problem about capacity that uses two of the four operations, then solve it step by step showing the operation chosen at each step.
What is a word problem, and what two things must you do when framing one from a mathematical statement?
Frame a word problem for the statement 80 / 4 = 20 and explain why your story matches the statement.

A student frames the statement 15 x 4 = 60 as: "There are 15 red balloons and 4 blue balloons. How many balloons are there in all?" Evaluate whether this is a correct word problem for the given statement, and explain what a better framing would look like.

Extract the hidden mathematical statement from this word problem: "A school bought 240 notebooks. They gave 150 to Class 4 and the rest to Class 5. How many notebooks did Class 5 get?" Show each step.
Write a two-operation word problem for the statement 20 x 3 + 10 = 70, using an Indian market or school context. Then verify it by solving.
State the rule for rounding a number to the nearest ten, and use it to round 47, 42, 35, and 68.
Estimate the sum 23 + 47 + 68 by rounding each number to the nearest ten, then explain why the estimate is close to the exact answer.

A student estimates 512 - 198 as 500 - 200 = 300, but a second student says "We should round only one number, so 512 - 198 is about 512 - 200 = 312." Evaluate both approaches and decide which gives a more reasonable estimate, with reasons.
A shopkeeper sells 4 notebooks at Rs 29 each. Estimate the total cost by rounding, then verify mentally whether your estimate is reasonable by comparing with the exact answer.

Design a short word problem set in an Indian market that requires estimating the sum of three item prices, round each price to the nearest ten, and explain how a child could verify the estimate mentally without paper.
What is a factor of a number? Find all the factors of 18 using multiplication facts and write them in order.
A student says the factors of 16 are 1, 2, 4, 8, and 16, but another student says 3 is also a factor of 16. Who is correct and why?
"Every number has at least two factors, so 1 must have two factors as well." Evaluate this statement. Is it correct? Explain your reasoning carefully.

A teacher has 24 pencils and wants to share them equally among a group of children so that no pencil is left over. List all the possible numbers of children the pencils can be shared among, and explain how this is connected to the factors of 24.

Design a short activity for a Class 4 student that uses 30 small objects (such as beads or buttons) to discover all the factors of 30 through equal grouping. Describe the steps and state the factors the student should find.
Define a multiple of a number and list the first five multiples of 6, showing the multiplication for each.

The multiples of 4 are 4, 8, 12, 16, 20, ... and the multiples of 6 are 6, 12, 18, 24, 30, .... Explain why 12 appears in both lists and identify what we call such a number. Find the next common multiple after 12.
A student says, "0 is the lowest common multiple of every pair of numbers, so the LCM of 5 and 7 is 0." Evaluate whether this claim is correct, giving a balanced argument.
On a number line, start at 0 and make jumps of 5. List the first six numbers you land on. Then use this list to find the LCM of 5 and 10.

Design a short story or real-life situation in which a shopkeeper uses multiples of 8 to arrange items, and use your story to explain how skip counting helps find the total number of items for 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 trays.
Define a prime number and a composite number, and state why 1 is neither.
The factors of 9 are 1, 3, and 9. A student says, "9 is odd, so it must be prime." Explain why the student is wrong and give the correct classification.

A classmate claims, "The number 1 should be called a prime number because it has no factors other than 1 and itself, just like 2, 3, and 5." Evaluate this claim. Do you agree? Give a balanced argument and a final judgement.
Classify each of the following numbers as prime, composite, or neither, by listing the factors and counting them: 11, 15, 1, 2, 21.

Design a small "prime detective" card game for your class. Describe the rules, give three example cards with their factor lists, and explain how the game teaches the difference between prime, composite, and the number 1.
In the number 4,52,316, state the place value and the face value of each digit.
Why is the place value of the digit 4 in 4,52,316 different from the place value of the digit 4 in 2,34,156, even though the face value is the same in both? Explain using the idea of position.

A student says, "In the number 2,38,905, the expanded form is 2,00,000 + 30,000 + 8,000 + 900 + 5, because the tens digit is 0 and 0 adds nothing, so we can leave it out." Evaluate whether this is correct, and explain whether leaving out the 0 term could ever cause a problem.
Reconstruct the number whose expanded form is 5,00,000 + 60,000 + 0 + 700 + 40 + 3. Show your steps and write the final number in the Indian system with the comma placed correctly.

Design a 6-digit number in the Indian system in which the digit in the lakhs place and the digit in the ones place have the same face value but very different place values, the tens place is 0, and the sum of all the place values is 6,05,408. Write the number, its expanded form, and the place value
State the divisibility rule for each of 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, and 10.
Using divisibility rules, determine whether 4368 is divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, and 10. Show the working for each test.

A student says, "Any number that is divisible by 9 is also divisible by 3, and any number divisible by 3 is also divisible by 9, because 9 and 3 are related." Evaluate this statement and explain whether it is fully correct, partly correct, or fully incorrect, with examples.
Without performing long division, list all the numbers from 230 to 250 that are divisible by both 3 and 4. Show the rule you applied for each.
Design a 4-digit number that is divisible by 2, 3, 4, 5, 9, and 10 all at once. Explain how you chose each digit so that every rule is satisfied, and verify your number with each rule.
What is a prime factor? Using the factor tree method, find the prime factorisation of 24 and verify your answer.
Two students factorise 60 using factor trees. Student A splits 60 as 2 x 30 first; Student B splits 60 as 6 x 10 first. Will they get the same prime factorisation? Explain why or why not.

A student claims that the prime factorisation of 36 is "36 = 4 x 9" and says this is correct because 4 x 9 = 36. Evaluate whether this claim is valid as a prime factorisation, and explain what a correct prime factorisation of 36 would look like.
Using the prime factorisation (division) method, find the prime factors of 84. Show each division step and verify your result by multiplying the prime factors back.

Design a factor tree for the number 72 in two different ways -- that is, using two different first splits -- and show that both ways give the same prime factorisation. Then write the final answer in product form.
Define the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of two numbers and state the two methods used to find it in Class 4.

Using the common division method, the steps for finding the HCF of 24 and 36 are: divide by 2 to get 12 and 18, divide by 2 again to get 6 and 9, divide by 3 to get 2 and 3. Explain why the HCF is 2 x 2 x 3 = 12 and not the product of the final quotients 2 x 3 = 6.

A student finds the HCF of 20 and 30 using the common division method. She divides both by 2 to get 10 and 15, and then stops, saying the HCF is 2 because that was the only divisor she used in the first step. She argues that since 10 and 15 are not both even, there is no point continuing. Evaluate w
Find the HCF of 28 and 42 using the listing method. Show all the factors of each number, identify the common factors, and state the HCF.

Design a real-life word problem in which finding the HCF of two numbers solves a practical problem. Use two numbers within the Class 4 range (up to 100), and show how the HCF gives the answer using either method.
Define the Lowest Common Multiple of two numbers and find the LCM of 5 and 10 using the listing method.
Explain why the LCM of 6 and 8 is 24 and not 12, using the idea of multiples and divisibility.
A student says, "The LCM of any two numbers is always their product, so the LCM of 4 and 6 is 4 x 6 = 24." Evaluate whether this statement is correct.
Find the LCM of 6 and 8 using the common division method, showing every step.

Two friends, Ananya and Bhavna, visit the school library every 4 days and every 6 days respectively. If both visit the library today, design a way to find after how many days they will next visit the library on the same day, and explain which method you would choose and why.
Name the seven pieces of a tangram and state how many of each type there are.
Two small triangles from the tangram are joined together along one of their equal sides. Explain what shapes can be formed and why the same two pieces can make different shapes.

A classmate says, "I made a tangram cat, but I only used six pieces because the parallelogram did not fit anywhere, so I left it out. My cat still looks fine, so it should be correct." Evaluate whether this is an acceptable tangram composition and explain your reasoning.
Using the outline of a large square drawn on paper (the size of the full tangram), show how all seven tangram pieces fit inside it. Describe where each piece goes.

Design an original tangram figure of your own -- for example, a bird, a fish, or a house -- using all seven pieces. Draw the outline and label each piece inside it. Describe how you decided which piece to use for each part.
Define tessellation and name three shapes that can tile a flat surface on their own.
Explain why a regular pentagon does not tessellate on its own but a regular hexagon does.
A student says, "A circle cannot tessellate, so no curved shape can ever be used in a tiling pattern." Evaluate this statement.

You are given a rectangular region and a set of square tiles and equilateral triangle tiles whose edges are all 4 cm long. Describe how you would tile the region using both shapes together so that there are no gaps and no overlaps.

Design your own tessellation pattern using two different shapes and describe it for a Class 4 friend who has never seen it. Explain which shapes you chose, why they fit, and where in real life such a pattern might appear.
Name the three parts of a circle -- centre, radius, and diameter -- and describe each in one sentence.
Why are all radii of the same circle equal in length? Explain using the definition of a circle.

A student draws a circle, marks a point O inside it, and draws a line from O to the circumference calling it the diameter. Another student says, "That is a radius, not a diameter." Evaluate who is correct and explain what the student who drew it should do to turn it into a proper diameter.
Using a compass, draw a circle of radius 5 cm. Mark the centre as O. Draw one radius and label it r. Draw the diameter and label it d. Describe each step you followed.
Design a paper-folding activity that helps a Class 4 student discover the centre, a radius, and a diameter of a circle without using a compass. List the steps and explain what each fold teaches.
State the two formulas that show the relationship between the diameter and the radius of a circle, and explain what each letter stands for.
The radius of a circular plate is 8 cm. Explain step by step how you would find its diameter, and then explain why your answer must be correct using what you know about the parts of a circle.

A student says, "If the diameter of a circle is 18 cm, then the radius is 36 cm, because the radius is bigger than the diameter -- it reaches all the way around." Evaluate whether this statement is correct. Give a balanced explanation of what the student got right, what the student got wrong, and ho

A circular lid has a diameter of 14 cm. Another circular disc has a radius of 9 cm. Find the radius of the lid and the diameter of the disc. Show your working and write the correct unit for each answer.

Design a simple classroom activity using a circular geoboard and rubber bands (or paper circles and folding) that would help a Class 4 child discover for themselves that the diameter is twice the radius. Describe the steps and what the child should observe.
What is reflection symmetry? Name the three activities suggested in the syllabus to explore it, and define the line of symmetry.
A square has four lines of symmetry but a rectangle has only two. Explain why a rectangle does not have diagonal lines of symmetry, using the fold-and-match test.
A classmate says, "The letter H and the letter X both have reflection symmetry, so they must have the same number of lines of symmetry." Evaluate this statement and give a balanced judgement.

Take a rectangular sheet of paper. Describe step by step how you would use the ink-blot method to produce a symmetric pattern, and then state how many lines of symmetry your finished pattern has if you folded the paper only once.

Design a paper-cutting activity for a Class 4 child that produces a symmetric Diwali rangoli motif with two lines of symmetry. Describe the steps, the shape you will cut, and how you will verify the symmetry.
Define perimeter and area in your own words, and state the unit used for each.
A rectangle is 6 cm long and 4 cm wide. Explain step by step how you would find both its perimeter and its area, and why the two answers are different numbers with different units.

A student says, "If two shapes have the same perimeter, they must also have the same area." Evaluate this statement using two rectangles, each with perimeter 16 cm, and explain whether the statement is correct.

The top of a table is covered with square tiles, each 1 unit by 1 unit. Along the length, 8 tiles fit; along the breadth, 5 tiles fit. There are no gaps and no overlapping. Find the perimeter and the area of the table top. Show your working.

Design a small rectangular kitchen garden for your school. Choose a length and a breadth in metres. Then describe how you would (a) measure its perimeter to buy fencing, and (b) measure its area to decide how many square planting tiles fit inside. Explain what could go wrong if you confuse perimeter
Define ascending and descending order. Arrange 2,34,567; 45,678; 1,23,456; 99,999 in ascending order and explain the first step you used.
Two numbers 3,45,678 and 3,45,687 have the same digits in five of their six places. Explain precisely at which place value the comparison is decided and why we do not need to look at the ones place.

A student says, "99,999 is greater than 1,00,000 because all its digits are 9, which is the biggest digit, while 1,00,000 starts with 1, which is the smallest digit." Evaluate this claim. Is the student correct? Explain the flaw in the reasoning and give the correct comparison.

A newspaper report lists the populations of four towns as 4,99,999; 5,00,000; 5,01,000; 4,98,999. Arrange these in descending order and identify the greatest and smallest town populations. Show the place value you used to decide the order.

Using number cards 0--9, a teacher asks you to design a set of five 6-digit numbers (using Indian comma notation) such that when arranged in ascending order, the comparison between the second and third numbers is decided only at the tens place, and the comparison between the fourth and fifth numbers
Name the three views used to describe a 3D object and state from which direction each view is seen.
A cuboid has length 6 cm, breadth 4 cm and height 2 cm. Explain what shape each of the three views will be and give the dimensions of each.
A student says, "Looking at just the front view of an object is enough to know its complete shape." Evaluate whether this statement is correct, giving a balanced argument.
The top view of an object shows a circle. List at least three different 3D objects that could produce this top view and explain how you would tell them apart using the front view.

Design a small quiz for your classmate with three "guess the object" questions based on views. For each question, describe the view you would show, the object it comes from, and the answer you expect.
Define a point, a line segment, a line, a ray, and parallel lines. Give one real-life example for each.
A figure shows a straight path with an arrowhead on only one end and a dot on the other end. Is it a line, a line segment, or a ray? Explain your reasoning.

A student says, "The two rails of a railway track are parallel because they are straight." Evaluate whether this statement is fully correct, and explain what else must be true for two lines to be called parallel.
Look around your classroom. List one real object or surface that matches each of these: a plane, a point, a line segment, a ray, and parallel lines. For each, say why it matches.

Design a simple poster titled "My Geometry World" that uses drawings and labels to teach all six terms -- plane, point, line, line segment, ray, parallel -- to a Class 3 student. Describe what you would draw and write for each term.
What are intersecting lines and perpendicular lines? How are they different?
Look at the letter X and the letter T. Both are made of two line segments that meet. Explain why one pair is perpendicular and the other is not.
A student says, "If two lines meet at a point, they must be perpendicular." Evaluate this statement and explain whether it is correct, partly correct, or wrong.
Using a ruler and a set square, describe step by step how you would draw a pair of perpendicular lines and mark the point of intersection.
Design a simple picture using only intersecting and perpendicular lines, and label which parts are intersecting (but not perpendicular) and which parts are perpendicular.
State the three fixed relationships between the unit pairs learnt in this node, and explain whether you multiply or divide when converting from a bigger unit to a smaller unit.
A shopkeeper has 3 kg 250 g of rice and 2750 g of flour. Which is heavier, and by how many grams? Show the conversion step.

A Class 4 child says, "To convert any bigger unit into a smaller unit, I always divide by 100, because that is the rule I remember from metres and centimetres." Evaluate whether this statement is correct, and explain what is wrong with it using all three unit pairs.
A water tank holds 6 litres of water. Riya fills it using a jug that holds 500 millilitres. How many jugfuls does she need to fill the tank completely? Show the conversion and the calculation.

Design a small measurement activity for your home in which you use all three unit pairs (m/cm, kg/g, L/mL) and write down one conversion each way (bigger-to-smaller and smaller-to-bigger) for every pair. List the objects you would measure.
State the standard units and conversions used for length, weight and volume at this stage, and name the four operations used to solve measurement word problems.

A shopkeeper has 3 kg 500 g of rice and sells 1 kg 200 g. Explain step by step how to find how much rice is left, and why converting to a single unit first is safer than subtracting kilograms and grams separately.

A student solves "A water tank holds 15 litres. If 3 buckets of 5 litres each are filled, how much water is used?" by writing 15 - 5 - 5 - 5 = 0 and concludes no water is left. Evaluate whether this approach and answer are correct, and explain what the question is actually asking.
A rope is 12 m long. It is cut into 4 equal pieces. What is the length of each piece? Show the full working with unit and a final answer sentence.
Write your own word problem involving volume (litres and millilitres) that requires two different operations to solve, and solve it showing all working.
What is estimation? What is verification? Name three standard units used for measuring length, weight and volume, and one instrument used to verify each.

A child estimates that a water bottle holds about 500 ml. When she pours the water into a measuring jug, it shows 480 ml. Explain whether her estimate was good, and state the difference between the estimate and the actual measurement.

A student says, "There is no point in estimating -- I should just measure everything directly with an instrument, because the instrument always gives the correct answer." Evaluate this statement. Do you agree? Give a balanced argument.

Estimate the length of your classroom in metres, the weight of your school bag in kilograms, and the capacity of a bucket in litres. For each, state which instrument you would use to verify your estimate, and describe how you would compare the estimate with the actual measurement.

Design a classroom "Estimation Station" with three activities -- one for length, one for weight, and one for volume. For each activity, describe the object to be estimated, the unit to be used, the instrument for verification, and how children will record and compare their results.
State the three fixed relationships between days, hours and minutes, and explain which operation (multiplication or division) is used to convert a bigger unit into a smaller unit and why.
A train leaves Howrah station at 16:40 and reaches Dhanbad at 20:10. Explain how to find the duration of the journey using the 24-hour clock, and convert both times into the 12-hour a.m./p.m. form.

A Class 4 student says, "I do not need to write a.m. or p.m. because the numbers on the clock already tell the time." Evaluate this statement, giving balanced reasons for and against, and state your final judgement.
Convert 2 days 7 hours into total hours, then convert 360 minutes into hours and minutes, and finally find the total time in hours if these two quantities are added together.

Design a simple one-day timetable for a Class 4 student that uses both the 12-hour a.m./p.m. form and the 24-hour clock form for each activity, and include at least two activities whose duration you calculate by subtraction.
Define time elapsed and name the four methods the syllabus gives for calculating it between two given times.
A movie starts at 4:15 p.m. and ends at 6:40 p.m. Explain step by step how you would find the duration using both forward counting and subtraction, and show that both methods give the same answer.

A student says, "From 9:30 a.m. to 1:10 p.m., I subtract 30 minutes from 10 minutes and get negative 20, so I just write 20 minutes, and then I subtract 9 from 1 and get negative 8, so the journey is 8 hours 20 minutes." Evaluate whether this method is correct, explain what is wrong, and show the co
School starts at 8:00 a.m. and ends at 2:30 p.m. Calculate the length of the school day using the subtraction method, showing all steps in neat columns.
Design your own word problem about time elapsed using a familiar Indian daily-life context. Give the start time, the end time, and the full worked solution using any one method.
What is raw data, and what are the three essential parts that every pictograph must have?

In a survey of 20 children, 8 like mango, 6 like apple, 4 like banana and 2 like grapes. Explain why a scale of "1 sticker = 2 children" is a better choice than "1 sticker = 1 child" for drawing this pictograph.

A student draws a pictograph of vehicles passing the school gate with the title "Vehicles" and rows labelled Car, Bike and Bus. She draws four car pictures of one size, three bike pictures of a larger size, and two bus pictures of a smaller size. She does not write any scale. Evaluate whether this p

The weather was observed for one week in Delhi. The results were: Sunny 3 days, Cloudy 2 days, Rainy 2 days. Draw a pictograph for this data using a suitable scale, a sun symbol for Sunny, a cloud symbol for Cloudy and a rain-drop symbol for Rainy. Show your working.

Design a small survey that you could carry out in your own classroom, and describe how you would collect the raw data and represent it as a pictograph. Include your title, categories, chosen symbol and chosen scale.
What are the main parts of a bar graph, and what does the height of each bar tell us?

A bar graph shows the number of ice creams sold from Monday to Friday: Monday 10, Tuesday 15, Wednesday 20, Thursday 12, Friday 18. On which day were the most ice creams sold, and how many more were sold on Wednesday than on Thursday?

A student looks at a bar graph and says, "I don't need to check the scale on the y-axis -- I can just count the divisions from the bottom to the top of each bar to get the value." Evaluate whether this approach is correct.
Collect data from your classmates about their favourite fruit among apple, banana, mango, and orange. Then draw a simple bar graph to show the data, with correctly labelled axes and a title.

Design a group project in which your class collects data about the number of absent students on each day of a week, and then represents it as a bar graph. Describe what data you would collect, how you would draw the graph, and what observations you could make from it.
Using the digits 3, 7, 1, 9, 0, 5, form the greatest and the smallest six-digit numbers. State the strategy in one line each.
Explain why 0,13,579 is NOT a valid six-digit number even though its digits are in ascending order, and state what the correct smallest six-digit number from the digits 3, 7, 1, 9, 0, 5 should be.

A classmate says, "From the digits 4, 4, 6, 2, 8, 8 with repetition allowed, the greatest six-digit number is 8,88,888 because 8 is the largest digit and I can repeat it six times." Evaluate this claim. Is the classmate correct? Give a balanced view of what the classmate got right and what went wron

You are given the digits 6, 0, 9, 3, 5, 1. Form the greatest and smallest six-digit numbers. Then write both numbers in the Indian place-value chart showing Lakhs, Ten-Thousands, Thousands, Hundreds, Tens, Ones.

Design a number-card game for four players using one set of cards 0 to 9. Each player draws six cards. Describe the rules, the scoring, and one sample round showing each player's greatest and smallest six-digit numbers. State how the game reinforces the leading-zero rule.
What is a growing pattern and what is a reducing pattern? Give one number example of each and state the rate of change.

Look at the shape pattern: triangle (3 sides), square (4 sides), pentagon (5 sides), hexagon (6 sides). Explain whether this is a growing or reducing pattern and how you know. What would the next shape be?

A student looks at the sequence 12, 10, 8, 6, 4 and says, "This is a growing pattern because the numbers are changing each time." Evaluate whether the student is correct. Explain what the student did wrong and give the correct classification and rate of change.

Here is a growing pattern: 5, 8, 11, 14, ... Extend the pattern by two more terms and describe the rate of change. Then make up your own reducing pattern that starts at 30 and has the same rate of change (by 3), and write its first five terms.

Design your own shape pattern that has more than one characteristic and is a growing pattern. Describe the two characteristics, state the rate of change, and draw or list the first four steps. Then explain in words how someone could tell it is a growing pattern.
What is a growing pattern and what is a reducing pattern? Give one example of each and state the rule for each.
For the pattern 3, 7, 11, 15, ..., explain step by step how you would formulate the rule, verify it, and extend it by two terms.

A child is given the pattern 2, 4, 6, 8, ... and says the rule is "multiply by 2 each time" because 2 x 2 = 4. Evaluate whether this rule is correct, and explain why verification across all terms matters.

A shape pattern begins with 1 square in step 1. In step 2, a row of 2 squares is added below. In step 3, a row of 3 squares is added below that. Draw or describe step 4 and step 5, and state the rule.
Create your own reducing number pattern of at least four terms, state its rule, verify it, and extend it by two more terms. Then create a growing shape pattern and describe its rule.
State the values of the symbols I, V and X, and write the Roman Numerals for 1, 5, 10, 4 and 9.
Explain why 4 is written as IV and not as IIII, but 3 is written as III and not as IV. What rule decides this?

A classmate says, "Since V means 5 and X means 10, the number 14 should be written as XIIV, because you put X for ten and then IV for four inside it." Evaluate whether this claim is correct, and explain what the proper Roman Numeral for 14 is and why.
Convert the following between Hindu-Arabic numerals and Roman Numerals: (a) 29 to Roman, (b) 38 to Roman, (c) XXIV to Hindu-Arabic, (d) XIX to Hindu-Arabic. Show your working.

Design a small poster for a Class 4 display board titled "My Roman Numerals Poster". Choose any five numbers between 1 and 39 that are not all simple additions (include at least two that use the subtraction rule), write each as a Roman Numeral, and next to each explain in one line which rule you use
What is a fraction? Name the three fractions you have learned and write their symbols. Also state what the numerator and the denominator tell us.

A square sheet of paper is folded twice and opened to show four parts, but one part is clearly bigger than the other three. A student shades the biggest part and calls it 1/4. Explain why this is not correct, and describe how the folding should be done so that 1/4 is truly shown.

A friend says, "Three-fourths and one-fourth are the same because both have a 4 in them, so it does not matter which symbol you write." Evaluate this statement. Is the friend correct? Give a balanced argument explaining when the two fractions might look similar and why they are actually different, w

Look at this situation: A basket has 12 flowers. Divide the flowers into four equal groups. (a) How many flowers are in one-fourth of the basket? (b) How many flowers are in three-fourths of the basket? (c) Write the symbols for both fractions and label the numerator and denominator in each.

Design a small activity for your class using a rectangular sheet of paper and a collection of 8 bottle caps that teaches all three fractions 1/2, 1/4 and 3/4. Describe each step, what the students will do, and what symbol they will write at each stage.
Define each of the four types of fractions -- like, unlike, unit, and equivalent -- and give one example of each.
Look at the pair 3/7 and 5/7. Explain why these are like fractions, and explain why 3/7 and 3/9 are not like fractions even though both have numerator 3.
A student says, "1/4 and 2/8 are the same fraction, so they are like fractions." Evaluate whether this statement is correct, giving a balanced argument.
Classify each of the following as one or more types and give your reason: (a) 1/6, (b) the pair 2/9 and 5/9, (c) the pair 1/3 and 2/6, (d) the pair 4/11 and 4/15.

Write three pairs of fractions of your own -- one pair of like fractions, one pair of unlike fractions, and one pair of equivalent fractions -- and for each pair explain in one sentence how you know it fits that type.
What are equivalent fractions? Using the example of 1/2 and 2/4, explain what makes them equivalent.

A strip of paper is folded into 6 equal parts and 3 parts are shaded, giving 3/6. Another identical strip is folded into 2 equal parts and 1 part is shaded, giving 1/2. Explain why these two fractions are equivalent by referring to the shaded lengths.

A student says, "2/4 must be greater than 1/2 because in 2/4 the numerator 2 is bigger than 1 and the denominator 4 is bigger than 2, so the fraction must be bigger." Evaluate this statement. Is the student correct? Give a balanced argument and conclude clearly.
Draw (or describe) how you would use paper folding and shading to show that 1/3 = 2/6. State the steps and what the result tells you.

Design a classroom activity for Class 4 students that uses paper folding and shading to discover a family of three equivalent fractions of your choice (not 1/2, 2/4, 3/6). Describe the materials, the steps the students will follow, and how they will record and explain their finding.
Add 3/7 + 2/7 and subtract 6/9 - 4/9. Show each step and state the rule you used.
Explain why, when adding 1/5 + 2/5, we keep the denominator as 5 and do not add the denominators to get 10.

A student says, "For 4/7 - 2/7, the answer is 2/0 because I subtract the tops and also subtract the bottoms: 4 - 2 = 2 and 7 - 7 = 0." Evaluate whether this reasoning is correct, and explain what the correct answer is and why.

A chocolate bar is divided into 8 equal pieces. Aarav eats 3 pieces and then his sister gives him 2 more pieces from the same bar. What fraction of the chocolate bar does Aarav have now? Write the fraction addition and solve.

Design a short story problem set in an Indian kitchen that involves both addition and subtraction of like fractions, with denominator 6. Write the problem, then solve it step by step, explaining each operation.
Write the 9-digit Indian place value chart and state the names of all four periods in order from left to right.
The number 7,89,23,456 is written in the Indian system. Explain step by step how you would convert it to the International system and state the number name in both systems.

A classmate says, "Since the Indian system has a Crores period and the International system has a Millions period, one crore and one million must be equal." Evaluate this statement. Is the classmate correct? Give a balanced argument and a clear verdict.

The average distance from Earth to Mars is about 22,79,00,000 km. (a) Write this number in the International system with correct commas. (b) State the number name in both systems. (c) Show how you would represent it on a 9-spike abacus.

Design a "two address formats" poster for the number 5,43,21,098. On one side show the Indian system with its place value chart, commas, and number name; on the other side show the International system with its chart, commas, and number name. Add one real-life context (such as a property price or a
What are the four operations used in Class 5 word problems, and which key question words usually signal each one?
A shopkeeper has 2450 pencils. He packs them into boxes of 25 each. Explain why the correct operation is division and not multiplication, and find the number of boxes.

A student solves "A school collected Rs. 3456 from each of 23 students for a trip. What is the total amount collected?" by writing 3456 / 23 and gets Rs. 150.26. Evaluate this solution, explain what went wrong, and give the correct solution with an estimation check.
Frame a word problem for the mathematical statement 2450 / 25 = 98, using a real-life Indian context, and then solve it showing the working and the answer sentence with the unit.

Design a short peer-exchange activity in which each child frames one word problem involving multiplication by a 2-digit number and one involving division by a 2-digit number, swaps with a partner, and checks the partner's work. Describe the rules, an example of each type of problem, and how the chec
List the seven Roman symbols used in Class V and state the value of each. Then write the six subtractive pairs and the number each represents.
Explain why 1987 is written as MCMLXXXVII and not as MDCCCCLXXXVII. Break the number into place values and justify each Roman group you use.

A student writes 950 as LM and argues that since L is 50 and M is 1000, putting the smaller L before the bigger M should mean 1000 minus 50, exactly the way IV means 5 minus 1. Evaluate this argument. Is the answer correct? Is the reasoning sound?
Convert the Roman numeral MMMCDXLVII into a Hindu-Arabic numeral. Show every group you identify and the running total.

Design a short poster for a Class V student that explains the seven Roman symbols and the subtraction rule using a memorable pattern. Include two worked examples of your own choice, one converting Hindu-Arabic to Roman and one converting Roman to Hindu-Arabic.
State the three rules of the standard algorithm for addition of large numbers and explain what "carrying" means in terms of place value.
In the subtraction 8,90,12,345 - 3,45,67,890, explain why you must borrow in the tens column and trace exactly what happens to the hundreds digit when you do.

A student says, "For multiplication, I can multiply by each digit of the multiplier and write all the partial products starting in the same ones column, then add them -- the answer will be the same as the standard algorithm." Evaluate whether this claim is correct, giving a balanced argument and a w
Calculate 12,345 x 23 using the standard algorithm, showing every partial product and every carry. Then verify your answer by an alternate method of your choice.

Design your own word problem set in an Indian context that requires adding two 8-digit numbers and multiplying a 5-digit number by a 2-digit number. Write the problem, solve it using the standard algorithm showing all working, and explain each carrying and borrowing step in your own words.
State the relationship between dividend, divisor, quotient, and remainder, and explain why the remainder must always be less than the divisor.
Divide 4368 by 12 using the standard long division algorithm and explain each step, including how you estimate each partial quotient.

A student divides 9450 by 25 using the breaking strategy as follows: 9450 = 9000 + 450, then 9000 / 25 = 360 and 450 / 25 = 18, so the answer is 360 + 18 = 378. Another student uses long division and gets 378. Evaluate whether both methods are valid, and discuss which method is more reliable and why
Divide 7856 by 23 using the standard long division algorithm, state the quotient and remainder, and verify your answer using the division relationship.

Design your own division problem with a five-digit dividend and a two-digit divisor that has a non-zero remainder, then solve it using both the standard long division algorithm and a breaking strategy (or a modified breaking strategy), and verify both answers match.
What are the four number operations used in framing and solving real life word problems, and what signal in a story tells you to use each one?
A school has 45 boxes of chalk with 144 sticks in each box. If 2,350 sticks are used in a term, how many sticks remain? Explain which operations you use and why, in the correct order.

A student framed this word problem for the statement 18,450 / 25 = 738: "There are 18,450 and 25. Find 738." Evaluate whether this is a well-framed problem, and explain what makes a word problem well-framed or poorly framed.
Frame a word problem for the statement 3,500 / 14 = 250, set in a real life context, and then solve it showing the working and the reasoning.

Create your own two-step word problem using both multiplication and subtraction, set in a real life context from your daily life, using large numbers. Then solve it and explain the reasoning for each step.
What is estimation? Explain how to estimate the sum 4,567 + 3,289 by rounding to the nearest 100, and verify your estimate against the exact answer.

Why does rounding to the nearest 10 give a closer estimate than rounding to the nearest 100 for the product 89 x 42, but rounding to the nearest 100 is better for the sum 4,567 + 3,289? Explain with calculations.

A student says, "Estimation is just a lazy way of doing maths and is never as good as finding the exact answer, so we should not learn it." Evaluate this statement, giving a balanced view and reaching a justified conclusion.

A school in Jaipur is taking 248 students on a field trip. Each bus can carry 40 students. Estimate the number of buses needed by rounding the number of students to the nearest 100, and verify your estimate by computing the exact number of buses.

Design a real-life estimation problem set in an Indian market that involves all four operations (sum, difference, product and quotient) on rounded numbers, and show the full working including verification.
What is a common denominator, and why is the LCM of the denominators the best choice when comparing three or more unlike fractions?
Compare 1/2, 2/3, and 3/4 by converting to equivalent fractions with a common denominator, and arrange them in ascending order. Explain each step.

A student says, "To compare 1/3, 2/5, and 1/4, I just look at the denominators -- 5 is the biggest denominator so 2/5 is the smallest fraction, and 3 is in the middle so 1/3 is in the middle, giving 2/5 < 1/3 < 1/4." Evaluate whether this reasoning is correct.
Arrange 3/5, 1/2, and 2/3 in descending order. Show the LCM, the equivalent fractions, and the final order.
Design a real-life story problem in which a child must compare three fractions to make a decision, and solve it using the LCM method.
Explain what unlike fractions are and state the four steps needed to add or subtract them.
Why must we find a common denominator before adding 1/3 and 1/4, and why is adding the denominators (giving 2/7) mathematically meaningless?

A student solves 5/6 - 1/4 by writing the answer as 4/2 = 2, explaining that "you subtract the numerators and subtract the denominators." Evaluate whether this method is correct, and discuss what it reveals about the student's understanding of fractions.
Calculate 2/5 + 3/4, showing every step, and express the answer both as an improper fraction and as a mixed number in lowest terms.
Design a real-life situation involving two unlike fractions that must be added, and solve it using the full common-denominator method. Explain each step in your own words.
What is a mixed number, and what are the two methods for adding or subtracting mixed numbers with unlike fractional parts?
Add 2 1/3 + 1 1/4 using the improper-fraction method, showing every step. Explain why the common denominator is 12.
A student solves 3 1/2 - 1 3/4 by writing: "3 1/2 - 1 3/4 = 2 (1/2 - 3/4) = 2 1/4." Evaluate whether this solution is correct, identify every error, and show the correct solution using both methods.
Add 1 2/5 + 2 1/3 using the separate-parts method, and subtract 4 1/6 - 2 2/3 using the improper-fraction method. Simplify both answers to lowest terms.

Design your own mixed-number addition problem and your own mixed-number subtraction problem (one that requires borrowing), then solve both using the method you think is best for each, explaining your choice of method.
State three key words in a word problem that signal addition and three that signal subtraction. Explain why a common denominator is needed before adding or subtracting unlike fractions.

A child solves "A bottle has 2 1/3 litres of juice. 1 3/4 litres are poured out. How much remains?" by writing 2 1/3 - 1 3/4 = 1 (1/3 - 3/4) = 1 something. Explain what is wrong and show the correct solution.

A student says, "Word problems on fractions are just the same as the sums we did before, so I do not need to write the story into a number sentence -- I can just look at the numbers and add them." Evaluate this claim, considering both what is correct and what is missing in the student's reasoning.
Solve this problem showing every step: "A tailor has 3 1/2 metres of cloth. He uses 1 2/5 metres for a shirt and 3/4 metre for a bag. How much cloth is left?"

Write your own word problem about addition or subtraction of unlike fractions or mixed numbers, set in a daily-life context of your home or school. Then solve it step by step, showing the common denominator and the simplified mixed-number answer with its unit.
In the number 54,32,10,987 written in the Indian system, state the place value and the face value of each of the digits 5, 3, and 7.

The same numeral 543210987 is written as 54,32,10,987 in the Indian system and as 543,210,987 in the International system. Explain why the digit 5 has a different place value in the two systems even though its face value is unchanged.

A student says, "The place value of a digit is always greater than its face value, except for zero." Evaluate whether this statement is fully correct, giving a balanced argument with examples from both the Indian and International systems.

Using a place value chart for the Indian system, place the digits of the number 8,07,56,432 and write down the place value and face value of the digits 8, 0, and 6. Then rewrite the same numeral in the International system and state the place value of the digit 8 in that system.

Design a "place value slider" activity using number cards and a place value chart that lets a Class 5 student discover for themselves how the place value of a single digit changes as it moves from the ones place to the crores place, while its face value stays the same. Describe the materials, the st
State the rule for multiplying a fraction by a whole number and the rule for multiplying a fraction by a fraction, with one example each.
Explain why 1/2 x 1/3 equals 1/6 and not 2/5, using the idea of the operation 'of' and a paper-folding illustration.

A student says, "Multiplication always makes numbers bigger, so 3/5 x 2/7 must be bigger than both 3/5 and 2/7." Evaluate this statement and explain whether the student is right or wrong, with a balanced discussion of when multiplication does and does not make numbers bigger.
Multiply 2/3 x 3/4 and simplify the result to its lowest terms. Show every step of your working, including any cancellation you do before multiplying.

Design a paper-folding activity that helps a Class 5 child discover the rule for multiplying 1/3 x 1/4. Describe the steps, what the child should observe at each stage, and how the activity leads to the rule "multiply numerators, multiply denominators."
State the rule for dividing a fraction by another fraction, and define the term reciprocal with one example.
Explain why 1/2 / 1/4 equals 2, using both the "how many fit" meaning and the reciprocal-and-multiply method. Why does the answer come out larger than the dividend?

A student says, "Division always makes the answer smaller, so 3 / 1/6 must be less than 3." Evaluate this claim. Is the student right or wrong, and why? Give a real-life example to support your reasoning.

Calculate 2/3 / 1/6 using the reciprocal-and-multiply method, showing every step. Then verify your answer by interpreting it as "how many 1/6 pieces fit into 2/3" using an origami paper-folding picture.

Design a short word problem set in an Indian kitchen that requires dividing a whole number by a fraction, and another that requires dividing a fraction by a fraction. Solve both, showing all steps and simplifying your answers.
What is a decimal fraction? Write 3/10, 7/100, and 9/1000 in decimal notation and explain which place each digit occupies.
Explain why 1/4 is equal to 0.25 and not 0.4. Show every step of the working.
A student says, "0.75 and 3/4 are two different numbers because one is a decimal and the other is a fraction." Evaluate this statement, giving a balanced argument and a final judgement.

A piece of ribbon is 7 cm 3 mm long and another piece is 4 cm 8 mm long. Express both lengths in centimetres as decimals, add them, and write the total first as a decimal and then as a fraction with denominator 10.

Design a small "fraction-decimal matching card" game for your class using six pairs of cards. Each pair must show the same value once as a fraction and once as a decimal. Include at least one fraction with denominator 1000, one common fraction (1/2, 1/4, or 1/5), and one money example. Explain how a
What is a pictorial representation of a decimal fraction, and which two grids are most commonly used in Class 5?
A 10x10 grid has 27 small squares shaded. Explain why the decimal represented is 0.27 and not 2.7, linking the shaded parts to the digits.
A student says, "I can show 0.6 by shading 6 parts in a 10x10 grid, because 6 out of 100 is the same as 0.6." Evaluate whether this statement is correct.
Draw (describe) how you would represent 0.45 on a 10x10 grid, and write the fraction and the explanation that goes with your diagram.
Design a short activity using origami paper that helps a Class 5 child discover that 0.3 and 0.30 represent the same amount. Describe the steps and what the child should conclude.
In the decimal 3.456, state the place value of each digit after the decimal point using both decimal and fractional notation.
Explain why 0.5, 0.50, and 0.500 represent the same value even though they have different numbers of digits after the decimal point.
A student says, "In 0.009, the 9 is in the tenths place because it is the first digit that is not zero, so its value is 9/10." Evaluate this statement and explain the correct reasoning.

A measuring tape is marked in metres, centimetres, and millimetres. A pencil's length is recorded as 0.075 m. State the place value of each digit after the decimal point, and express the length in centimetres and millimetres using the metric sub units deci, centi, and milli.

Design a small place-value chart (a table with columns) for the decimal 2.384, labelling each column with its place name, the digit, the fractional value, and the matching metric sub unit for a length measured in metres. Then write the number in expanded form.
Write 234.67 in expanded form and name the place value of each digit.
Reconstruct the decimal number from the expanded form 8/10 + 4/100 + 5/1000, and explain why the answer has no whole-number part.
A student writes 15.3 = 10 + 5 + 3/100. Evaluate whether this is correct, and explain what the error tells us about the student's understanding of place value.

Using a measuring tape marked in centimetres and millimetres, explain how a length of 7.4 cm can be written in expanded form. Then reconstruct 6/10 + 4/100 back into a decimal and state what length it represents in centimetres.

Design a small "decimal shop" activity in which three items are priced in decimal rupees (for example, one item at 12.5, one at 0.75, and one at 3.06). For each price, write the expanded form using fractions, and explain how you would pay each amount using Indian currency notes and coins (rupees, te
Define equivalent, like, and unlike decimals with one example each.
Explain why 0.7, 0.70, and 0.700 are equivalent but 0.7 and 0.07 are not. Use place value in your answer.

A student says, "0.6 and 0.60 are like decimals because they both contain the digits 6 and 0, and they are also equivalent because they look almost the same." Evaluate this statement by separating the correct part from the incorrect part, and explain the difference between like and equivalent decima
Convert the unlike decimals 7.5, 3.825, and 12.06 into like decimals. Show each step and state the number of decimal places in the result.

Design a small card game for your class that uses number cards 0 to 9 and a decimal-point card. The game must let players practise (a) forming equivalent decimals, (b) classifying decimals as like or unlike, and (c) converting unlike decimals to like decimals. Describe the rules and give one full ro
State the three steps for comparing two decimal fractions and explain why unlike decimals must be converted to like decimals first.
Compare 0.508 and 0.55 by converting to like decimals and comparing digit by digit. Explain each step.
A student says, "0.9 is smaller than 0.89 because 9 is smaller than 89." Evaluate this claim. Is the student correct? Explain why or why not, and give the correct comparison with full working.
Compare the three decimal fractions 0.4, 0.45, and 0.455. Arrange them with the correct symbols between each pair and show all working.

Design a short "decimal comparison challenge" with three pairs of decimal fractions for a classmate. One pair should be equivalent decimals, one pair should need conversion from unlike to like decimals, and one pair should require comparison up to the thousandths place. Provide the full worked solut
What are like decimals and unlike decimals, and why must we convert unlike decimals to like decimals before ordering them?
Arrange 2.3, 2.03, and 2.345 in descending order and explain which place value decided the order between 2.3 and 2.345.

A student arranges 0.6, 0.06, and 0.6 in ascending order as 0.06, 0.6, 0.6 and writes "0.6 and 0.6 are equal so the order does not matter." Another student arranges them as 0.06, 0.6, 0.6 but insists the first 0.6 must come before the second 0.6 because it appeared first in the question. Evaluate bo
Arrange the following decimal fractions in ascending order, showing the like-decimal conversion and stating which place value decided the order: 0.5, 0.55, 0.505, 0.055.

Design a set of four decimal fractions (each with up to three decimal places) that would be tricky for a classmate to order, and write a short explanation of why your set is tricky and what mistake you hope it would catch.
State the rule for adding or subtracting decimal fractions, and explain what is meant by converting unlike decimals to like decimals.
Why must 2.3 be written as 2.30 before adding it to 3.45, and what would go wrong if we added them without converting?

A student says, "Annexing zeros to make like decimals is a waste of time -- I can just add 5.6 and 3.47 by lining up the right-hand ends, the way I do for whole numbers, and I get 8.13 which is close enough." Evaluate this claim, stating whether the student is right or wrong and giving a balanced ex
Work out (a) 4.56 - 1.8 and (b) 0.125 + 0.4, showing the conversion to like decimals and the column working in each case.

Design a short worksheet of three addition and three subtraction problems using decimals with up to three decimal places, where each problem requires converting unlike decimals to like decimals. For each problem, write the full worked solution showing the conversion and the aligned column working.
Write 5,43,21,098 in expanded form using the Indian system and explain what each term represents.
Reconstruct the compact form of 2,00,00,000 + 0 + 50,000 + 0 + 300 + 0 + 5 and explain why the zero terms matter.

A student writes the expanded form of 5,43,21,098 as 5,00,00,000 + 40,00,000 + 3,00,000 + 20,000 + 1,000 + 900 + 8 and claims it is correct because "the 9 is still there." Evaluate this claim, identify the error, and explain its consequence.
Write 123,456,789 in expanded form using the International system, then rewrite the same number in the Indian system and expand it again. Compare the two expansions.

Design a place-value-card activity for a Class 5 student that practises both expanding and reconstructing a 9-digit number with at least two zero digits. Describe the cards, the steps, and a self-check method.
What three steps must you follow to solve a word problem on addition or subtraction of decimal fractions? Give one example of a clue word that tells you to add and one that tells you to subtract.
A bag of rice weighs 5.25 kg and a bag of flour weighs 3.8 kg. The shopkeeper says the total weight is 8.105 kg. Explain why the shopkeeper is wrong and give the correct total weight.

A student says, "In every word problem with decimals, I should always add the numbers because the question gives me two decimal quantities." Evaluate this statement. Is the student correct? Give a balanced argument with at least two examples.

Solve this problem showing all working: A water tank contains 25.6 litres of water. A family uses 7.85 litres in the morning and 6.4 litres in the afternoon. How much water is left in the tank? (Hint: this needs two steps.)

Write your own word problem on subtraction of decimal fractions using a real-life situation from your home or school. Include the clue words that tell the reader to subtract, show the full working, and state the answer with the correct unit.
State the rule for multiplying a decimal fraction by 10, 100, and 1000, and explain why the rule works using place value.
Explain why 0.07 x 100 equals 7 and not 0.7, using both the shift rule and the fraction method.

A student says, "Multiplying a decimal by a power of 10 changes the digits themselves, so 2.36 x 10 should give a number with different digits like 23.6 written as 24.0 because the digits must grow." Evaluate this claim and explain what actually happens to the digits and to the decimal point.
Calculate each of the following and show the shift in each case: (a) 3.45 x 10, (b) 0.6 x 100, (c) 12.05 x 1000, (d) 0.009 x 100.

Design a short story or a shop analogy that explains the shift rule to a younger child, using at least three examples -- one each for multiplication by 10, 100, and 1000 -- with specific decimal numbers and their products.
State the rule for placing the decimal point in the product when multiplying a decimal number by a whole number or by another decimal number.
Explain why 0.2 x 0.3 equals 0.06 and not 0.6, using the idea of place value.

A student says, "When I multiply 1.5 by 0.6, I get 9.0, because 15 x 6 = 90 and I keep one decimal place from 1.5." Evaluate whether this method is correct, and explain what the right answer is and why.
A shopkeeper sells 12 pens at Rs. 2.45 each. Calculate the total cost using the decimal-place counting rule, showing each step.

Design a short word problem about finding the area of a rectangular field whose length and width are both decimal numbers, with a total of three decimal places across the two dimensions. Then solve it using the rule.
List all the factors of 36 and explain how you know you have not missed any.
The factors of 30 are 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 10, 15, 30 and the factors of 45 are 1, 3, 5, 9, 15, 45. Explain why the HCF of 30 and 45 is 15 and not 5, even though 5 is a common factor.

A student finds the HCF of 24 and 36 by common division. She divides both by 2 to get 12 and 18, then by 2 again to get 6 and 9, then by 3 to get 2 and 3. She then multiplies 2 x 2 x 3 x 2 x 3 = 72 and says the HCF is 72. Evaluate whether her method and answer are correct.
Find the HCF of 42 and 56 using the common division method, showing every step neatly. Then verify your answer using the listing method.

Design a short word problem about two Indian school groups packing sweets into equal boxes, where finding the HCF solves the problem. State the two numbers, solve it, and explain why the HCF is the answer rather than any other common factor.
Write the first five multiples of 7 using the multiplication table, and explain what a multiple is.
Two buses arrive at a bus stop -- bus A every 4 minutes and bus B every 6 minutes. If both arrive together at 0 minutes, after how many minutes will they next arrive together, and why?

A student finds the LCM of 12 and 18 by common division. They divide both by 6 to get 2 and 3, then stop and say the LCM is 6 x 2 x 3 = 36. Another student divides both by 2 to get 6 and 9, then by 3 to get 2 and 3, then stops and says the LCM is 2 x 3 x 2 x 3 = 36. Evaluate both methods and explain
Find the LCM of 8 and 12 using (a) the listing method and (b) the common division method. Show all steps.
Design a short word problem for a Class 5 student in which finding the LCM of two numbers solves a real-life situation. State the two numbers, solve it, and explain why the LCM is the answer.
Define a prime number and a composite number, and give one example of each with its factors listed.
Explain why (11, 13) is a twin prime pair but (7, 11) is not, even though all four numbers are prime.
A student says, "8 and 15 cannot be co-prime because both are composite numbers, and co-prime numbers must be prime." Evaluate this statement and explain whether the student is correct.
List all the prime numbers between 30 and 50. Then, from that list, identify any twin prime pairs. Finally, check whether 34 and 35 are co-prime by listing their factors.

Design a small "prime detective" game for your class using the numbers 1 to 30. Describe how a classmate would play it, what clues you would give for prime, composite, twin prime, and co-prime, and give one example of a correct answer for each category.
What is a prime factor, and when is a factor tree considered complete?
Two students build factor trees for 72. Student A splits 72 as 8 x 9 first. Student B splits 72 as 6 x 12 first. Will they get the same prime factors? Explain why.

A student writes the prime factorisation of 60 as 60 = 2 x 6 x 5 and says the factor tree is complete. Evaluate whether this answer is correct, explain what is wrong, and describe how you would help the student fix it.
Draw a factor tree for 96 and express 96 as a product of its prime factors. Show at least two different ways of splitting and confirm both give the same answer.

Design a factor tree challenge for a classmate using a three-digit number of your choice. Write the number, show one correct factor tree, give the prime factorisation, and then write one deliberately wrong factor tree that a confused student might make. Explain exactly what is wrong with the wrong t
Define the Highest Common Factor and state the two methods used to find it for two numbers.
Using the common division method, find the HCF of 48 and 72. Show every step and explain why you stop where you do.

A student says, "For finding the HCF of 96 and 144, the listing method and the common division method are equally good because they give the same answer." Evaluate this statement, considering accuracy, time, and the kinds of errors each method tends to produce.
Find the HCF of 84 and 120 using the common division method, and verify your answer by checking that it divides both numbers exactly.
Design a short word problem set in an Indian market where a shopkeeper must use the HCF to decide something practical, and show how a Class 5 student would solve it using the common division method.
Define the Lowest Common Multiple of two numbers and name the two methods used to find it in this node.
Find the LCM of 12 and 18 using the common division method, showing every step, and explain why multiplying the divisors gives the LCM.

A student says, "For any two numbers, the listing method and the common division method are equally efficient, so I will always use the listing method because it is easier to understand." Evaluate this statement.
Find the LCM of 15 and 20 using both the listing method and the common division method, and show that both give the same answer.
Design a short word problem set in an Indian market that requires finding an LCM, choose the more efficient method for your numbers, and solve it.
State the relationship between the HCF and LCM of two numbers, and write it as a formula.
Verify the relationship HCF x LCM = product of the two numbers for the pair 15 and 20, showing every step.
A student says, "Since HCF x LCM = product of the two numbers, I can always find the LCM of any two numbers by multiplying them and dividing by the LCM." Evaluate whether this statement is correct.
The HCF of two numbers is 8 and their LCM is 48. If one of the numbers is 16, find the other number.

Design a short worksheet of two pairs of numbers for a Class 5 friend, where for each pair you give the HCF and one number, and ask your friend to find the LCM using the relationship. Include the answer key with full working.
